ami_style_notes:
The meeting has a relaxed, collegial video-call style with mostly short to medium turns, though speakers give long, structured presentation monologues. Before and between formal segments, participants use casual small talk, frequent greetings, light joking, and loosely connected follow-ups. Overlap and interruptions are fairly common but generally cooperative—brief acknowledgments, “yeah”s, and quick interjections rather than aggressive interruptions. Speech is highly disfluent in places, with fillers (“um,” “uh,” “yeah”), repetitions, self-corrections, false starts, and unfinished phrasing, especially from non-native speakers. Formality shifts noticeably: introductions and presentations are semi-formal and appreciative, while discussion is conversational and permissive. Questions are often prefaced with praise, hedges, or self-deprecation (“quick question,” “naive question,” “I’m curious”), then develop into multi-part exploratory questions. Challenges are indirect and framed as curiosity or requests for clarification; speakers respond generously, admitting uncertainty and identifying open questions rather than asserting absolute conclusions. Participants build on prior comments by restating part of the previous point, connecting it to their own work, and offering future collaboration.

Meeting style for this meeting (tangent_heavy): The conversation drifts. Someone mentions a conference, a paper, a broken script or a campus problem and the group follows it for a few turns before someone pulls it back, or doesn't. The main topic still gets covered but unevenly.
Illustration of the feel only (invented, do not reuse the wording or topic):
  - Wait, did that reviewer thing ever get sorted out?
  - Oh god, no. Anyway, sorry- what were we saying about the sites?
  - No, go on, I want to hear about the reviewer.
Opening: Start with one person apologizing for being a couple of minutes late and asking where the group has got to.
Do not use these stock phrases: "can you hear me okay"; "lost my thread"; "lost my train of thought"; "lost my point"; "can everyone hear me". The recording does not need to begin with audio or login checks.
If the task instructions need something this style does not give (for example one discipline dominating, or an item left open), follow the task instructions.
research_problem: Redesigning catch limits for a community-managed reef fishery so stocks recover without pushing families out of fishing.

speakers.name: Leilani Faumuina
speakers.background: Fourth-year marine ecology PhD candidate with five years of field experience in Indo-Pacific reef fisheries. Her work combines underwater visual census, spawning-aggregation observations, habitat transects, and fisher-assisted landing sampling to relate reef condition to population recovery. She has previously worked with community monitors but has not led a full catch-limit design process.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Leilani treats catch limits as a biological safeguard that must be grounded in evidence about abundance, size structure, spawning timing, habitat condition, and fishing pressure across reefs. She will emphasize comparable May-July observations, a common landing-record format, and documentation of bycatch and fishing locations before drawing conclusions about stock status. She is wary of using incomplete market records as a proxy for total removals, and wants local tenure guidance before field teams enter sites or interpret differences among reefs.
speakers.language_complexity: plain — avoids jargon, explains concepts simply

speakers.name: Mateo R. Villanueva
speakers.background: Third-year environmental economics PhD candidate specializing in small-scale fisheries, household livelihoods, and policy incentives. He has designed stated-preference and household-budget modules in coastal communities and uses panel-style surveys, price-series analysis, and scenario modeling to estimate distributional effects of harvest rules. He is comfortable co-designing survey instruments with local partners and revising models when administrative data prove incomplete.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Mateo sees a catch limit as a distributional and behavioral policy, not only a total-harvest number. He will ask which households rely on fishing income, food fish, reciprocal transfers, tourism, or farming; how catch and prices vary; and how alternative allocations affect both welfare and willingness to comply. He needs a usable dataset that separates sales, household use, and gifts, but accepts that who counts as a fisher and how household information can be collected must be established with community guidance before economic sampling begins.
speakers.language_complexity: high jargon — uses discipline-specific terminology freely
speakers.epistemic_stance: open to other perspectives, willing to revise

speakers.name: Dr. Mereana Taukolo
speakers.background: Senior anthropologist with 16 years of research and advisory work on customary marine tenure, kinship, gendered labor, and participatory governance in Pacific island coastal communities. Her methods include long-form ethnographic observation, semi-structured interviews, genealogy-informed social mapping, and facilitated community discussions. She has supported fisheries projects but remains attentive to the ways technical surveys can misclassify people, rights, and obligations.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Mereana approaches the fishery as a set of social relationships and rights rather than a simple list of boat owners or individual harvesters. She will prioritize mapping tenure groups, access authority, shore-based and kin-linked fishing labor, and sharing obligations that shape how fish and income circulate. She will insist that the team first establish locally acceptable definitions of participation and consent-sensitive procedures for household data collection, because those decisions determine valid sampling lists and whether proposed rules will be seen as legitimate.
speakers.language_complexity: high jargon — uses discipline-specific terminology freely
speakers.epistemic_stance: uncertain about how their methods apply to this problem

seed_spec.explicit_instruction: Hold a planning meeting with one ecologist, one economist, and one anthropologist. The group must agree on coordinated research next steps needed before an August 2027 community review, while keeping the proposed catch-limit design open. The ecologist explains that May-July spawning observations, standardized landing sampling, bycatch records, and reef-condition surveys are needed to estimate stock status and identify biologically sensitive places and periods. The economist explains that household income sources, catch and price variation, likely effects of alternative quota allocations, and incentives for compliance must be assessed; these estimates depend on a usable catch and household-use dataset. The anthropologist explains that the team must map customary tenure, determine who should be counted as participating in fishing and fishing-related labor, document sharing obligations, and establish acceptable ways to collect household data; this work must occur before finalizing sampling lists or household surveys. The participants should assign clear owners, dates, dependencies, and a method for integrating findings. They should decide that anthropology-led tenure and fisher-definition work begins first in May; ecology begins spawning and reef observations in May and uses locally validated site access information; economics co-designs a household and landing-data instrument with anthropology after initial definitions are validated, then begins data collection in June. Ecology and economics share a standardized landing record, but the group must not claim that existing market records are sufficient. The team should schedule a late-July synthesis session and prepare alternative catch-limit scenarios, rather than choosing a final limit during this meeting. No conflict is required: all participants accept the need for the dependencies and joint review.

ground_truth.agreed_scope: Develop evidence and alternative catch-limit scenarios for an August 2027 community review; do not select a final catch limit yet.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mereana Taukolo
transcript.text: Oh, apologies, I’m a couple of minutes late—where have we got to? Um, if we’re just starting, I was hoping today we could work out the sequencing for May, particularly what has to be established with the tenure groups before anyone treats boat owners as a sampling frame.

transcript.speaker: Mateo R. Villanueva
transcript.text: I think that has to come first. For the household side especially, I need to know whether the meaningful unit is a residence, a tenure-group household, or a wider kin network that shares fish and income. Otherwise we'll misread both dependence and who bears a lower limit. Mereana, what's the least intrusive way to establish that in May?

transcript.speaker: Leilani Faumuina
transcript.text: Mm, yeah, that matters.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mereana Taukolo
transcript.text: I’d begin with separate, small conversations with the relevant tenure groups—not a household enumeration yet. We need to ask who may authorize access, who they regard as contributing to fishing, and whether information about transfers or obligations can be held at group level; then we can build a provisional social map and have them correct it. I should check with the council first on the proper sequence, because convening the wrong people first can itself be read as taking a position.

transcript.speaker: Mateo R. Villanueva
transcript.text: And that sequence also tells us whether repeated visits in June are even workable. Tourism shifts and farm work may make a conventional household panel pretty awkward. Once you've checked the council protocol, could we- could we ask in those early conversations what counts as an appropriate way to record fish that moves through kin, instead of treating every transfer as an individual household transaction?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mereana Taukolo
transcript.text: I'd frame that as a question about categories and permissions, not ask people to itemize every gift. Is fish given through particular relationships reportable at household level, aggregated for a tenure group, or just described qualitatively? And that same conversation needs to surface whether the shoreline work distinction I heard is broadly meaningful, household labour versus a tenure-group obligation, because that changes what your instrument is actually measuring, and...

transcript.speaker: Mateo R. Villanueva
transcript.text: That’s not a small wording issue for us. If shoreline labour or kin obligations are part of the claim on a catch, then modeling allocation only around the person landing fish could shift costs onto people we never observe. Could the May conversations also tell us whether people would be comfortable separating fish for meals, gifts, and cash sale at all, or whether those categories blur in particular situations?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mereana Taukolo
transcript.text: We should ask, but not presume the meal, gift, sale distinction is the locally salient one. Fish may be caught for one purpose and then redistributed through an obligation, so the June instrument may need room for a pathway instead of forcing a single endpoint. I’ll need the tenure-group conversations to tell us whether it’s even appropriate to ask that at household level.

transcript.speaker: Mateo R. Villanueva
transcript.text: A pathway field makes more sense than a destination variable. For the welfare model, I can still construct disposition measures later, but only if we record the sequence. It would be caught, then maybe first intended use, then what actually moved where. I was going to say that without implying a kin transfer is just an off-market sale. And I’m also wondering whether the tenure groups will see price information as similarly sensitive, since the preliminary notes have this odd pattern where the biggest fish aren’t consistently getting the highest price.

transcript.speaker: Leilani Faumuina
transcript.text: That price pattern could be mixing sites and fishing methods too, not just buyer preferences. For the May to July sampling, I’d want to record where it was caught, the species, size, and gear, alongside whatever people are comfortable saying about where the fish went. Otherwise, a large fish from a spawning site and one from another reef just end up in the same price column.

transcript.speaker: Mateo R. Villanueva
transcript.text: The landing record has to carry those ecological covariates, otherwise any price estimate is doing too much work. If we can settle the permitted categories in late May, I'd like to have the joint landing-and-household instrument running in June. Then we can use the late-July synthesis to compare allocation scenarios instead of just proposing one aggregate cap.

transcript.speaker: Leilani Faumuina
transcript.text: That timing sounds workable if the access conversations happen before we lock the sites in. I’d want the same landing form running through June and July, though, not just June, because the spawning observations need repeated coverage across all three reefs. Otherwise we’re trying to turn one month into a limit before 1 September. I still need to check staffing and, uh, tide windows for that.

transcript.speaker: Mateo R. Villanueva
transcript.text: June and July is better, otherwise we'd miss both the seasonal catch composition and the price movement around the aggregations. Leilani, by late July, which biological indicators do you think will be stable enough to put alongside alternative caps or reef-specific allocations? I don't want the welfare scenarios to imply more precision than the ecology can support.

transcript.speaker: Leilani Faumuina
transcript.text: Probably not a defensible stock number, honestly. By late July, we can compare relative abundance and size structure across the three reefs, and see whether the spawning groups are being hit. We can put that alongside habitat condition and reported effort, but I’d use it as evidence for cautious scenarios, not a precise cap. That live-coral reef with fewer large fish is exactly why I don’t want to assume habitat alone explains the—

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mereana Taukolo
transcript.text: That uncertainty matters for August. We shouldn't present a biologically exact ceiling and then ask the council to ratify it. If the alternatives are explicitly precautionary, could we frame them reef by reef? Could the access authorities then say whether a restriction is socially workable, as well as ecologically indicated?

transcript.speaker: Leilani Faumuina
transcript.text: Reef by reef is the right way to show it, as long as we don't imply a reef is open to a particular rule before the tenure groups say how that would work. We can bring- actually, bring a few precautionary options tied to what we actually observe, especially protection during the spawning period and different levels of removal, not a single number dressed up as certainty.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mereana Taukolo
transcript.text: The reef-by-reef approach may not line up neatly with the social unit that can deliberate or enforce. Before August, I need to know whether rights overlap across those reefs, and whether a seasonal closure of a spawning area puts a particular burden on people whose access is otherwise limited. We can present the ecological options spatially, but the council discussion may need to be organized through the relevant tenure- it may need to go through the relevant tenure authorities, rather than simply by reef.

transcript.speaker: Mateo R. Villanueva
transcript.text: For the allocation scenarios, I probably shouldn’t map a household to one reef just because that’s where a landing was recorded. We may need to model the burden at the access-group level first, then ask how it distributes through households and shoreline labour. Otherwise a spatial closure looks equitable in the spreadsheet and is not, um, equitable in practice.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mereana Taukolo
transcript.text: I’d be careful even with “access group” as if it’s a settled analytic unit. It may be, but we need people to tell us whether rights, labour, and redistribution line up that way or cross-cut it. I can try to get that initial mapping validated before Mateo fixes those scenarios. Otherwise, we may make a very tidy model out of categories nobody...

transcript.speaker: Mateo R. Villanueva
transcript.text: Mm, let's not freeze it yet.

transcript.speaker: Leilani Faumuina
transcript.text: Until that mapping is validated, I’d keep the biological comparison separate from any claim about why the reefs differ. On the landing form, we can document location and effort, plus bycatch. But that coral-and-large-fish mismatch could be about access or fishing pressure, rather than reef condition. At this point, we just don’t know.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mereana Taukolo
transcript.text: Mm. That's why I'd avoid asking a respondent to explain the reef difference in the instrument itself. It can invite blame, especially where access is contested. We can record the locally accepted place and effort categories, but I need to find out first whether naming a particular reef or spawning area is sensitive. Or whether that information should sit with the tenure authority rather than travel on an individual landing form. I was going to say we can just record it, but that depends on whether it's sensitive first.

transcript.speaker: Leilani Faumuina
transcript.text: If reef names or exact aggregation locations are sensitive, we can code the locations on the field sheets and keep the key with the authorized group, instead of putting that detail into the shared landing dataset. I just need enough consistent spatial resolution to tell whether the spawning observations and landings are coming from the same general area. Mereana, is that the kind of arrangement the council might accept?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mereana Taukolo
transcript.text: Possibly, yes, but I really can't promise it until I've asked the council how authority over those names and the resulting records is meant to sit. A coded sheet with the key controlled by the appropriate authority sounds like a useful starting proposal. I'd want to ask whether the code can be reported at a broader reef-sector level where an exact site would expose a tenure- where it would expose a tenure claim.

transcript.speaker: Mateo R. Villanueva
transcript.text: I think we should leave it there before people have to run. I’ll follow up by email once we’ve got the council protocol piece a little clearer, and then we can—

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mereana Taukolo
transcript.text: All right. Goodbye, both.

transcript.speaker: Leilani Faumuina
transcript.text: Thanks—talk soon.
